reconcile.connective: Defenders count Jehoiachin's three-month vassal reign as too slight to register, so Jeremiah's 'none to sit upon the throne' stands without conflict.

discrepancy.connective: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible presses the plain contradiction: 2 Kings says Jehoiakim's son Jehoiachin reigned in his stead, yet Jeremiah swore Jehoiakim would have no one on David's throne.

skeptic.name: Skeptic's Annotated Bible (Steve Wells)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999– )

excerpts.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
excerpts.work: Commentary Critical and Explanatory on the Whole Bible
excerpts.excerpt_text: The very brief reign of this prince, which lasted only three months, during which he was a humble vassal of the Assyrians, is scarcely deserving to be taken into account, and therefore is in no way contradictory to the prophetic menace denounced against his father (Jer 36:30).
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Names the contradiction explicitly and resolves it: Jehoiachin's three-month reign is too slight to count, so it does not falsify Jeremiah's word that Jehoiakim would have none on the throne. The most direct of the three harmonizing voices.

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats the Jehoiakim succession under the harmonizing tradition that a three-month vassal reign ending in deportation is not a true sitting upon David's throne.

link.title: Jeremiah 36:30—How can this verse say that Jehoiakim shall have no one to sit on the throne when his son reigned after him?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment arguing the Hebrew 'sit on the throne' connotes a permanent enthronement Jehoiachin never achieved in his three-month reign.
